title: Platform Frameworks: Maps, Media, Payments, Widgets
scopeHtml: Scope: MapKit, CoreLocation, Camera and PhotosUI, StoreKit 2, WidgetKit, App Intents, Sign in with Apple, HealthKit overview.

notes.title: Baseline and the framework map
notes.html:
Android equivalent. On Android, platform features come from Google Play services (Maps, Location via FusedLocationProvider, Play Billing, Sign-In) plus AOSP APIs (CameraX, App Widgets, App Actions). On iOS almost everything is a first-party framework shipped inside the OS and imported by name: no Play-services-style separate update channel, no Gradle dependency, but also no way to patch the framework without an OS update.

Baseline for every note in this track. Swift 6 language mode, Xcode 16+, iOS 17/18 minimum deployment target, SwiftUI-first with UIKit where a framework still needs it, @Observable, async/await, actors, Swift Testing. Legacy forms (completion handlers, ObservableObject, delegates) are shown only as "you will meet this in old codebases". Anything new in iOS 18/26 is marked verify.

Android iOS
Google Maps SDK / Maps Compose MapKit (Map in SwiftUI)
FusedLocationProviderClient CoreLocation (CLLocationManager, CLLocationUpdate)
CameraX AVFoundation (AVCaptureSession)
Photo Picker (PickVisualMedia) PhotosPicker (PhotosUI)
Play Billing Library StoreKit 2
App Widgets / Glance WidgetKit (SwiftUI only)
Foreground service notification / ongoing notification Live Activities (ActivityKit)
Credential Manager / Google Sign-In Sign in with Apple (AuthenticationServices)
App Actions / shortcuts App Intents
Google Pay Apple Pay (PassKit)
Health Connect HealthKit
ML Kit / TFLite Core ML, Vision

How to add a framework. import MapKit is enough for system frameworks (they are linked automatically via modules). Capabilities (Sign in with Apple, HealthKit, Push, App Groups for widgets) are switched on in the target's Signing & Capabilities tab, which edits the .entitlements file and the provisioning profile. Missing capability is a classic "works in simulator, fails on device" bug.

Real industry examples. Uber and Lyft use CoreLocation heavily with custom accuracy tiers; Airbnb uses MapKit-style clustering over its own tiles in places; Duolingo and Spotify ship widgets; Strava uses HealthKit and CoreLocation.

Analogy. Android feels like shopping at a market where Google Play services is the big anchor stall plus many independent stalls. iOS is a department store: everything is in one building and the store decides when it restocks.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "iOS has no equivalent of Play services": it is the OS itself, versioned with iOS, which is why you gate with @available.
  • Forgetting capabilities and Info.plist keys; the app compiles and then crashes or silently fails at runtime.
  • Mixing up entitlements (signed, grant privileges) with Info.plist (declares strings and metadata).

notes.title: CoreLocation permissions and accuracy
notes.html:
Android equivalent. You request ACCESS_COARSE_LOCATION / ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION at runtime, then ACCESS_BACKGROUND_LOCATION separately, and read fixes from FusedLocationProviderClient with a LocationRequest priority. On iOS the same split exists, but the user-facing model is "While Using" vs "Always" plus a one-time "Allow Once" option and a reduced-accuracy toggle.

Mechanism. CLLocationManager owns authorization and delivers fixes. The user sees a system prompt whose explanatory text comes from Info.plist. The key is mandatory: a missing NSLocationWhenInUseUsageDescription makes the request do nothing (or the app is rejected in review).

<key>NSLocationWhenInUseUsageDescription</key>
<string>We show nearby stores and give you walking directions.</string>
<key>NSLocationAlwaysAndWhenInUseUsageDescription</key>
<string>Needed to keep delivery tracking running while the app is closed.</string>

Authorization states (CLAuthorizationStatus): .notDetermined, .restricted (parental controls, user cannot change), .denied, .authorizedWhenInUse, .authorizedAlways. Accuracy authorization (CLAccuracyAuthorization) is .fullAccuracy or .reducedAccuracy: the user can grant only an approximate area (roughly several kilometres, verify exact radius), and you can ask for temporary full accuracy with requestTemporaryFullAccuracyAuthorization(withPurposeKey:) using a key declared in NSLocationTemporaryUsageDescriptionDictionary.

Modern API (iOS 17+): an AsyncSequence of updates, no delegate.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
import CoreLocation

@MainActor
@Observable
final class LocationModel {
    private let manager = CLLocationManager()
    var latest: CLLocation?
    var status: CLAuthorizationStatus = .notDetermined

    func requestAccess() {
        manager.requestWhenInUseAuthorization()   // shows the system prompt once
    }

    func start() async {
        do {
            for try await update in CLLocationUpdate.liveUpdates() {
                if let loc = update.location { latest = loc }
                if update.authorizationDenied { status = .denied; break }
            }
        } catch {
            // CLError; treat as transient
        }
    }
}
class LocationRepo(private val client: FusedLocationProviderClient) {
    fun updates(): Flow<Location> = callbackFlow {
        val req = LocationRequest.Builder(Priority.PRIORITY_HIGH_ACCURACY, 5_000).build()
        val cb = object : LocationCallback() {
            override fun onLocationResult(r: LocationResult) { r.lastLocation?.let(::trySend) }
        }
        client.requestLocationUpdates(req, cb, Looper.getMainLooper())
        awaitClose { client.removeLocationUpdates(cb) }
    }
}

Legacy form you will meet: CLLocationManagerDelegate with locationManagerDidChangeAuthorization(_:) and locationManager(_:didUpdateLocations:). Still required for region monitoring in older code.

Accuracy and battery. desiredAccuracy takes kCLLocationAccuracyBest, ...NearestTenMeters, ...HundredMeters, ...Kilometer, ...ThreeKilometers, and ...Reduced. Higher accuracy keeps GPS on and burns battery. Cheaper alternatives: startMonitoringSignificantLocationChanges() (cell-tower scale, wakes a terminated app), region monitoring with CLCircularRegion/CLMonitor (iOS 17+), and distanceFilter to suppress tiny updates.

Background location. Needs the capability Background Modes > Location updates, allowsBackgroundLocationUpdates = true, and (iOS 11+) the blue status-bar pill. CLBackgroundActivitySession (iOS 17+) keeps a SwiftUI app alive for location. "Always" is requested after "When In Use"; the OS shows an "Always" prompt later, and may downgrade silently. Apple reviewers reject apps asking for Always without a clear need.

Real examples. Uber requests While Using, later upgrades to Always for trip safety features. Strava uses background location during activity recording. Life360 relies on significant-change plus region monitoring.

Analogy. Authorization is a visitor badge: day pass (Allow Once), office hours (While Using), 24/7 (Always), and a blurry-photo badge (reduced accuracy).

Common interview traps.

  • Calling requestAlwaysAuthorization() first: iOS expects When-In-Use first, Always as a later upgrade.
  • Checking CLLocationManager.locationServicesEnabled() on the main thread (it blocks; call it off main in legacy code).
  • Assuming .denied can be re-prompted: you must send the user to Settings via UIApplication.openSettingsURLString.
  • Android mix-up: "coarse vs fine" is a per-app permission choice on Android 12+, while on iOS it is the single .reducedAccuracy switch.

notes.title: MapKit with SwiftUI
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Maps Compose wraps the Google Maps SDK: GoogleMap { Marker(...) } with CameraPositionState. iOS ships Apple Maps in MapKit, free for app use, no API key, with a native SwiftUI Map from iOS 17.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
import SwiftUI
import MapKit

struct StoreMap: View {
    @State private var position: MapCameraPosition = .userLocation(fallback: .automatic)
    let stores: [Store]
    @State private var selected: Store.ID?

    var body: some View {
        Map(position: $position, selection: $selected) {
            UserAnnotation()
            ForEach(stores) { store in
                Marker(store.name, systemImage: "cart.fill", coordinate: store.coordinate)
                    .tag(store.id)
            }
            MapCircle(center: stores[0].coordinate, radius: 500)
                .foregroundStyle(.blue.opacity(0.2))
        }
        .mapControls { MapUserLocationButton(); MapCompass() }
        .mapStyle(.standard(elevation: .realistic))
    }
}
@Composable
fun StoreMap(stores: List<Store>) {
    val camera = rememberCameraPositionState()
    GoogleMap(cameraPositionState = camera, properties = MapProperties(isMyLocationEnabled = true)) {
        stores.forEach { Marker(state = MarkerState(it.latLng), title = it.name) }
        Circle(center = stores[0].latLng, radius = 500.0, fillColor = Color(0x330000FF))
    }
}

Pieces to know.

  • MapCameraPosition (.region, .camera, .item, .userLocation, .automatic), bound via Map(position:).
  • Content builders: Marker, Annotation (custom SwiftUI view), MapPolyline, MapPolygon, MapCircle, UserAnnotation.
  • Search: MKLocalSearch and MKLocalSearchCompleter (autocomplete). Directions: MKDirections returning MKRoute, drawn with MapPolyline(route).
  • Open in the Maps app: MKMapItem.openInMaps(launchOptions:).
  • Look Around (street-level): MapItemDetail/LookAroundPreview in newer SDKs (verify).
  • Pre-iOS 17 you will see Map(coordinateRegion:annotationItems:) or a UIViewRepresentable wrapping MKMapView with MKMapViewDelegate. MKMapView is still the tool for thousands of annotations and clustering (MKClusterAnnotation, clusteringIdentifier).

Performance. Hundreds of SwiftUI Annotation views are fine, thousands are not; cluster or fall back to MKMapView with reusable annotation views (dequeueReusableAnnotationView), the same reuse idea as RecyclerView.

Real examples. Airbnb and Zillow show hundreds of pins with clustering; many food-delivery apps use MapKit on iOS and Google Maps on Android, then pay a cost in visual inconsistency. Google Maps SDK for iOS is also available if the product demands parity (needs an API key, and key restriction by bundle id).

Analogy. MapKit is the city map pinned in the lobby; Google Maps SDK is renting the same map from a company that ships it to every building.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing MapKit needs an API key or billing: it does not (but has usage throttling on search/directions, verify limits).
  • Using Map(coordinateRegion:) in new code; it is deprecated in favour of MapCameraPosition.
  • Updating @State position from the onMapCameraChange closure in a loop, causing an update storm.
  • Mixing up latitude/longitude order when porting from Android LatLng(lat, lng): CLLocationCoordinate2D(latitude:longitude:) is labelled, so errors are rarer, but GeoJSON is lng,lat.

notes.title: AVFoundation camera basics
notes.html:
Android equivalent. CameraX gives ProcessCameraProvider, Preview, ImageCapture, ImageAnalysis bound to a lifecycle. iOS gives AVCaptureSession with inputs, outputs and a preview layer; there is no lifecycle binding, you start and stop it yourself.

AVCaptureDevice (back wide camera) -> AVCaptureDeviceInput ->
        AVCaptureSession  -> AVCapturePhotoOutput   (stills)
                          -> AVCaptureVideoDataOutput (frames for ML, like ImageAnalysis)
                          -> AVCaptureMovieFileOutput (video)
        AVCaptureVideoPreviewLayer shows the session on screen

Permission: NSCameraUsageDescription in Info.plist (and NSMicrophoneUsageDescription for audio). Check/request:

import AVFoundation

func cameraAllowed() async -> Bool {
    switch AVCaptureDevice.authorizationStatus(for: .video) {
    case .authorized: return true
    case .notDetermined: return await AVCaptureDevice.requestAccess(for: .video)
    default: return false   // .denied, .restricted -> send user to Settings
    }
}

Session setup with Swift 6 in mind: AVCaptureSession is not Sendable, and startRunning() blocks, so confine it to one serial queue or an actor.

final class CameraService: NSObject, @unchecked Sendable {
    let session = AVCaptureSession()
    private let output = AVCapturePhotoOutput()
    private let queue = DispatchQueue(label: "camera.session")   // all session work here

    func configure() {
        queue.async { [session, output] in
            session.beginConfiguration()
            session.sessionPreset = .photo
            guard let device = AVCaptureDevice.default(.builtInWideAngleCamera, for: .video, position: .back),
                  let input = try? AVCaptureDeviceInput(device: device),
                  session.canAddInput(input), session.canAddOutput(output) else {
                session.commitConfiguration(); return
            }
            session.addInput(input); session.addOutput(output)
            session.commitConfiguration()
            session.startRunning()          // blocking: never on main thread
        }
    }
}

Showing the preview in SwiftUI needs a UIViewRepresentable whose layer class is AVCaptureVideoPreviewLayer (SwiftUI has no native camera preview). Capture with output.capturePhoto(with: AVCapturePhotoSettings(), delegate: self) and receive photoOutput(_:didFinishProcessingPhoto:error:); photo.fileDataRepresentation() returns JPEG/HEIC data. Barcode/QR scanning uses AVCaptureMetadataOutput; for documents consider VisionKit's DataScannerViewController (iOS 16+) or VNDocumentCameraViewController.

Gotchas. The simulator has no camera, so test on a device. Orientation is handled through AVCaptureConnection rotation (iOS 17 videoRotationAngle; older videoOrientation, verify). Interruptions (phone call, Split View on iPad) post AVCaptureSession.wasInterruptedNotification.

Real examples. Instagram and Snapchat write their own capture pipelines on AVCaptureVideoDataOutput plus Metal for filters; banking apps use VNDocumentCameraViewController for cheque capture.

Analogy. A session is a film set: you pick the camera (input), decide where the footage goes (outputs), then shout "action" (startRunning).

Common interview traps.

  • Calling startRunning() on the main thread: causes a main-thread hang warning and UI freezes.
  • Missing NSCameraUsageDescription: the app terminates immediately on first access, a very common crash.
  • Expecting CameraX-style lifecycle awareness; you must stop the session on backgrounding.
  • Capturing in .photo preset and then wondering why frame rate for analysis is low.

notes.title: PhotosPicker and photo library access
notes.html:
Android equivalent. The Android Photo Picker (ActivityResultContracts.PickVisualMedia) returns URIs without storage permissions. iOS PhotosPicker (PhotosUI, iOS 16+) is the same idea: out-of-process picker, no permission prompt, the app only sees what the user selects.

Languages: Swift · Kotlin
import SwiftUI
import PhotosUI

struct AvatarPicker: View {
    @State private var item: PhotosPickerItem?
    @State private var image: Image?

    var body: some View {
        PhotosPicker(selection: $item, matching: .images) {
            image?.resizable().scaledToFill().frame(width: 96, height: 96).clipShape(.circle)
                ?? Image(systemName: "person.crop.circle.badge.plus")
        }
        .onChange(of: item) { _, newItem in
            Task {
                if let img = try await newItem?.loadTransferable(type: Image.self) { image = img }
            }
        }
    }
}
val launcher = rememberLauncherForActivityResult(PickVisualMedia()) { uri: Uri? ->
    uri?.let { viewModel.setAvatar(it) }
}
Button(onClick = { launcher.launch(PickVisualMediaRequest(PickVisualMedia.ImageOnly)) }) { Text("Pick") }

Details.

  • PhotosPickerItem.loadTransferable(type:) is async; Data.self gives raw bytes, Image.self a SwiftUI image (loses metadata). Prefer Data, then downsample with CGImageSourceCreateThumbnailAtIndex to avoid decoding a 48 MP image fully (memory spike, jetsam risk).
  • maxSelectionCount: 5 for multi-select. matching: .any(of: [.images, .videos]).
  • Full library access (PHPhotoLibrary, PHAsset) requires NSPhotoLibraryUsageDescription and offers .limited access (iOS 14+) where the user picks a subset; the system re-prompts periodically. Use it only for gallery-like apps.
  • Saving to the library needs only NSPhotoLibraryAddUsageDescription (add-only).
  • Legacy: UIImagePickerController (still used for the camera source) and PHPickerViewController (UIKit wrapper behind PhotosPicker).

Real examples. WhatsApp, Slack and Notion all use the out-of-process picker for attachments; Instagram needs full library access for its custom gallery grid.

Analogy. The picker is a vending window: you ask for a photo, the staff behind the glass fetches only the one you choose, and never lets you into the stockroom.

Common interview traps.

  • Requesting library permission just to let the user pick one image: unnecessary and review-unfriendly.
  • Loading full-size UIImage for a thumbnail, producing memory warnings.
  • Forgetting loadTransferable can fail (iCloud download, unsupported type): handle throws and show progress.
  • Treating .limited as .denied.

notes.title: StoreKit 2: subscriptions and in-app purchase
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Play Billing Library: BillingClient, queryProductDetails, launchBillingFlow, PurchasesUpdatedListener, then acknowledgePurchase within three days or Google refunds. StoreKit 2 (iOS 15+) is Swift-native, async/await based, and returns cryptographically signed JWS transactions the device already verifies.

Concept Play Billing StoreKit 2
Fetch catalogue queryProductDetailsAsync try await Product.products(for: ids)
Buy launchBillingFlow(activity, params) try await product.purchase()
Updates stream PurchasesUpdatedListener Transaction.updates (AsyncSequence)
Acknowledge/consume acknowledgePurchase, consumeAsync await transaction.finish()
Restore queryPurchasesAsync Transaction.currentEntitlements, AppStore.sync()
Server validation Play Developer API purchase tokens App Store Server API + Server Notifications V2
Test license testers StoreKit configuration file, Sandbox, TestFlight 
import StoreKit

@MainActor
@Observable
final class Store {
    var products: [Product] = []
    var entitled: Set<String> = []
    private var updatesTask: Task<Void, Never>?

    init() {
        updatesTask = Task { [weak self] in
            for await result in Transaction.updates {            // renewals, refunds, Ask-to-Buy approvals
                await self?.handle(result)
            }
        }
    }

    func load() async throws {
        products = try await Product.products(for: ["pro.monthly", "pro.yearly"])
    }

    func buy(_ product: Product) async throws {
        switch try await product.purchase() {
        case .success(let verification): await handle(verification)
        case .pending: break          // Ask to Buy / SCA: wait for Transaction.updates
        case .userCancelled: break
        @unknown default: break
        }
    }

    private func handle(_ result: VerificationResult<Transaction>) async {
        guard case .verified(let tx) = result else { return }   // never grant on .unverified
        entitled.insert(tx.productID)
        await tx.finish()
    }

    func refreshEntitlements() async {
        var ids: Set<String> = []
        for await result in Transaction.currentEntitlements {
            if case .verified(let tx) = result, tx.revocationDate == nil { ids.insert(tx.productID) }
        }
        entitled = ids
    }
}

Product types. Consumable, non-consumable, auto-renewable subscription (grouped into subscription groups so a user holds one tier at a time; upgrade/downgrade/crossgrade rules), non-renewing subscription. Subscription features: introductory offers (free trial), promotional offers, offer codes, Product.SubscriptionInfo.status for renewal state, grace period and billing retry. SwiftUI helpers: SubscriptionStoreView and StoreView (iOS 17+) give a ready paywall.

Rules that bite.

  • Digital goods consumed inside the app must use Apple IAP (guideline 3.1.1); Apple takes 30% (15% for Small Business Program and for subscriptions after year one). Regional rules differ (EU, US link-out rulings, Japan), so mark verify per market and date.
  • A Restore Purchases control is required for non-consumables and subscriptions.
  • Server side: trust the App Store Server API and App Store Server Notifications V2 (signed JWS), not the client, for entitlement on web/Android. appAccountToken links a transaction to your user id.
  • Legacy: StoreKit 1 (SKPaymentQueue, SKProduct, receipt validation with verifyReceipt) – deprecated; you will meet it in old code. RevenueCat wraps both and is widely used for cross-platform entitlements.

Real examples. Spotify and Netflix steered users away from in-app signup historically; Duolingo, Headspace, Calm run auto-renewable subscriptions with trials and RevenueCat or an in-house backend.

Analogy. A purchase is a signed cheque: StoreKit 2 hands you the cheque already stamped by the bank (JWS); your job is to check the stamp and cash it once (finish).

Common interview traps.

  • Not listening to Transaction.updates at launch, losing renewals, Ask-to-Buy approvals and out-of-app purchases.
  • Forgetting finish(), so the transaction replays every launch.
  • Android mix-up: there is no 3-day acknowledge deadline; instead, unfinished transactions persist.
  • Trusting .unverified results or client-side flags without server validation.

notes.title: WidgetKit timelines
notes.html:
Android equivalent. App Widgets use RemoteViews, an AppWidgetProvider, and updatePeriodMillis (minimum 30 min) or WorkManager; Glance gives a Compose-like API. WidgetKit widgets are SwiftUI views rendered from a timeline of snapshots that the system prepares ahead of time; the widget is not a running process.

App (main process) ---writes data---> App Group container (shared UserDefaults / file)
                                              |
Widget extension: TimelineProvider -> [Entry t0, Entry t1, ...] -> system renders views
        reload policy: .atEnd | .after(date) | .never
App triggers refresh: WidgetCenter.shared.reloadTimelines(ofKind:)
import WidgetKit
import SwiftUI

struct ScoreEntry: TimelineEntry { let date: Date; let score: Int }

struct Provider: TimelineProvider {
    func placeholder(in: Context) -> ScoreEntry { .init(date: .now, score: 0) }
    func getSnapshot(in: Context, completion: @escaping (ScoreEntry) -> Void) { completion(.init(date: .now, score: 42)) }
    func getTimeline(in: Context, completion: @escaping (Timeline<ScoreEntry>) -> Void) {
        let score = SharedStore.currentScore()                        // read from App Group
        let entries = (0..<4).map { ScoreEntry(date: .now.addingTimeInterval(Double($0) * 900), score: score) }
        completion(Timeline(entries: entries, policy: .after(.now.addingTimeInterval(3600))))
    }
}

struct ScoreWidget: Widget {
    var body: some WidgetConfiguration {
        StaticConfiguration(kind: "ScoreWidget", provider: Provider()) { entry in
            Text("\(entry.score)").containerBackground(.fill.tertiary, for: .widget)
        }
        .supportedFamilies([.systemSmall, .systemMedium, .accessoryCircular])
    }
}

Newer AppIntentTimelineProvider replaces IntentTimelineProvider (SiriKit intents) for configurable widgets (iOS 17+). Interactive widgets (iOS 17+) allow Button(intent:) and Toggle(isOn:intent:) that run an AppIntent without opening the app.

Key facts.

  • Widget is a separate app extension target with its own memory limit (tens of MB, verify) and no long-running code; data sharing needs an App Group.
  • Refresh budget is system-controlled (rough guidance is on the order of 40 to 70 reloads a day per widget, verify); .atEnd and .after are hints, not guarantees. Push-triggered reload via WidgetPushHandler (iOS 17+, verify).
  • Families: systemSmall/Medium/Large/ExtraLarge, lock screen accessoryCircular/Rectangular/Inline; iOS 18 adds controls (ControlWidget, verify).
  • Cannot do scrolling, video, or arbitrary animations; links use widgetURL / Link.

Real examples. Weather apps (Carrot, Apple Weather) pre-compute hourly entries; Duolingo's streak widget reads a shared streak count; Todoist uses interactive intents to complete a task.

Analogy. A widget is a printed timetable posted at a bus stop: you print the schedule in advance for the next hours, you do not stand there updating it live.

Common interview traps.

  • Expecting getTimeline to run on every home-screen view: it runs when the system decides.
  • Network calls with long timeouts inside getTimeline, killing the extension.
  • Forgetting App Group entitlements on both app and extension, so the widget shows stale or empty data.
  • Android mix-up: you cannot update a widget on a timer you control.

notes.title: Live Activities (verify details)
notes.html:
Android equivalent. An ongoing foreground-service notification (or Android 16 live-update notifications, verify) shows a ride or delivery in progress. On iOS, ActivityKit (iOS 16.1+) puts a live card on the Lock Screen and in the Dynamic Island (iPhone 14 Pro and later), updated by the app or by push.

import ActivityKit

struct DeliveryAttributes: ActivityAttributes {
    struct ContentState: Codable, Hashable { var eta: Date; var status: String }
    var orderId: String                         // static part
}

func startDelivery() throws {
    let attrs = DeliveryAttributes(orderId: "A-1")
    let state = DeliveryAttributes.ContentState(eta: .now.addingTimeInterval(1500), status: "Preparing")
    let content = ActivityContent(state: state, staleDate: nil)
    _ = try Activity.request(attributes: attrs, content: content, pushType: .token)   // token for server updates
}

The UI is declared in the widget extension with ActivityConfiguration(for:) supplying lock-screen view and DynamicIsland { expanded / compact / minimal }. Updates come from the app (activity.update(...)) or APNs push with apns-push-type: liveactivity using the activity push token. Limits (verify): up to about 8 hours of activity life plus a few hours on the lock screen after end; a payload size cap around 4 KB; update budget with an optional high-frequency entitlement NSSupportsLiveActivitiesFrequentUpdates.

Real examples. Uber (ride ETA), DoorDash, Apple Sports, Flighty use server-pushed updates; Zomato and Swiggy on iOS follow the same pattern.

Analogy. A scoreboard that the stadium operator updates by radio: your app does not need to be awake, the server shouts new numbers.

Common interview traps.

  • Updating from the app only: when suspended, the activity goes stale; real products push.
  • Putting large images in state; payload is tiny, use asset names.
  • Starting activities in the background without the proper push-to-start flow (iOS 17.2+, verify).

notes.title: Sign in with Apple and its App Store requirement
notes.html:
Android equivalent. Credential Manager with Google ID tokens, or "Sign in with Google". Apple's version uses AuthenticationServices and returns an identity token (JWT) your backend verifies against Apple's public keys.

The rule. App Store guideline 4.8: if your app offers a third-party or social login (Google, Facebook, etc.), it must also offer an equivalent privacy-preserving login option; Sign in with Apple is the usual choice (alternatives that limit data to name and email, allow email hiding, and avoid ad tracking also qualify). Exemptions: your own first-party account system only, enterprise/education logins, government IDs. Wording has changed over time; verify current text.

import SwiftUI
import AuthenticationServices

struct LoginView: View {
    var body: some View {
        SignInWithAppleButton(.signIn) { request in
            request.requestedScopes = [.fullName, .email]      // returned ONLY the first sign-in
        } onCompletion: { result in
            switch result {
            case .success(let auth):
                guard let cred = auth.credential as? ASAuthorizationAppleIDCredential,
                      let tokenData = cred.identityToken,
                      let jwt = String(data: tokenData, encoding: .utf8) else { return }
                Task { try await AuthAPI.exchange(appleUserId: cred.user, identityToken: jwt) }
            case .failure(let error):
                print(error)    // ASAuthorizationError.canceled is normal
            }
        }
        .signInWithAppleButtonStyle(.black)
        .frame(height: 48)
    }
}

Details.

  • credential.user is a stable, per-team opaque id. Name and email arrive only on the first authorization; persist them immediately. The email may be a private relay address (...@privaterelay.appleid.com).
  • Backend verifies the JWT (iss https://appleid.apple.com, audience your bundle id, signature via Apple's JWKS) and checks the nonce you sent.
  • On launch call ASAuthorizationAppleIDProvider().getCredentialState(forUserID:) (.authorized, .revoked, .notFound, .transferred) and listen to credentialRevokedNotification.
  • Account deletion: since June 2022 apps with account creation must offer in-app deletion; with Sign in with Apple you must also revoke the token via the REST API (guideline 5.1.1(v)).
  • Capability: add Sign in with Apple in Signing & Capabilities.

Real examples. Airbnb, Uber and Pinterest offer it next to Google/Facebook. Many apps reviewed after adding Facebook login but forgetting Apple login get rejected under 4.8.

Analogy. It is a hotel key card that hides your home address: the hotel (app) gets a working key and a forwarding mailbox, never your real details.

Common interview traps.

  • Assuming email and name are available on every sign-in.
  • Sending a bare user id to the backend instead of a verified identity token.
  • Shipping Google login without Apple login and getting a 4.8 rejection.
  • Forgetting token revocation during account deletion.

notes.title: App Intents, Siri and Shortcuts overview
notes.html:
Android equivalent. App Actions (actions.xml with built-in intents) and static/dynamic shortcuts via ShortcutManager, plus Assistant. On iOS, App Intents (iOS 16+) is a Swift-only framework that exposes actions and data to Siri, Shortcuts, Spotlight, widgets, the Action button and Apple Intelligence (iOS 18, verify scope). It replaces SiriKit INIntent definition files for most uses.

import AppIntents

struct AddTaskIntent: AppIntent {
    static let title: LocalizedStringResource = "Add Task"
    static let description = IntentDescription("Adds a task to your list.")

    @Parameter(title: "Title") var taskTitle: String

    func perform() async throws -> some IntentResult & ProvidesDialog {
        try await TaskStore.shared.add(taskTitle)
        return .result(dialog: "Added \(taskTitle).")
    }
}

struct AppShortcuts: AppShortcutsProvider {
    static var appShortcuts: [AppShortcut] {
        AppShortcut(intent: AddTaskIntent(),
                    phrases: ["Add a task in \(.applicationName)"],
                    shortTitle: "Add Task", systemImageName: "plus")
    }
}

Building blocks. AppIntent (an action), AppEntity + EntityQuery (the nouns Siri can resolve, e.g. a playlist), AppEnum, AppShortcutsProvider (phrases available without user setup), openAppWhenRun, IntentDialog, and @Dependency for injecting services. Intents run in the app process or an extension; keep perform() quick. Donation and Spotlight indexing use IndexedEntity and CSSearchableItem (verify newest API names).

Real examples. Things and Todoist expose "add task", Spotify and Apple Music expose "play"; Home-automation apps use entities for rooms.

Analogy. Intents are the menu you hand to the OS: "here is what I can do and what I need", and any restaurant guide (Siri, Shortcuts, Spotlight) can then order for the user.

Common interview traps.

  • Confusing App Intents (Swift, in-target) with legacy SiriKit (Intents definition file, extension).
  • Making perform() do long network work without timeouts; the system aborts it.
  • Expecting phrases to work in every language; phrases must be localised.

notes.title: Apple Pay, HealthKit and Core ML overview
notes.html:
Apple Pay (PassKit). Android equivalent: Google Pay API. For physical goods and services only (digital goods use IAP). You need a Merchant ID and a payment processing certificate from your PSP (Stripe, Adyen, Braintree). Flow: PKPaymentRequest (merchantIdentifier, countryCode, currencyCode, supportedNetworks, merchantCapabilities, paymentSummaryItems) presented by PKPaymentAuthorizationController or SwiftUI PayWithApplePayButton. The delegate receives an encrypted PKPayment.token, which you forward to the PSP; you never see the card number. Test with sandbox cards in Wallet. Real use: Uber, Instacart, Shopify checkouts.

HealthKit. Android equivalent: Health Connect. Capability HealthKit, plus NSHealthShareUsageDescription (read) and NSHealthUpdateUsageDescription (write). Data is typed (HKQuantityType(.stepCount)), read via HKHealthStore queries (HKStatisticsCollectionQuery, HKSampleQuery, HKAnchoredObjectQuery) or the async descriptors (HKStatisticsQueryDescriptor, iOS 15.4+). Key privacy quirk: for read permissions the app is deliberately not told whether the user denied, to avoid leaking health state. Background delivery via enableBackgroundDelivery. Apps cannot use HealthKit data for advertising. Real use: Strava, MyFitnessPal, Oura.

Core ML. Android equivalent: TensorFlow Lite / ML Kit. Convert a model with coremltools into .mlpackage; Xcode generates a typed Swift class; inference runs on CPU, GPU or the Neural Engine chosen by MLModelConfiguration.computeUnits. High-level frameworks cover common tasks without a custom model: Vision (text, faces, barcodes), Natural Language, Speech, Sound Analysis. Use Create ML for training small models on a Mac. Newer on-device LLM access through Apple Foundation Models (iOS 26, verify). Real use: Photos search, Snapchat lenses, Pinterest visual search.

Analogy. These are three government counters: payments (Apple Pay) hands you a sealed envelope, health (HealthKit) will answer only the questions you were licensed to ask, and ML (Core ML) is the calculator built into the phone.

Common interview traps.

  • Using Apple Pay for in-app digital subscriptions (rejected; must be IAP).
  • Treating a HealthKit read result of "no data" as "permission denied" (they are indistinguishable by design).
  • Running big models on CPU only and blaming Core ML; check computeUnits and Instruments' Core ML template.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Each Android capability has a first-party iOS framework imported by name; capabilities (entitlements) and Info.plist usage strings are mandatory, and missing ones crash or silently fail.
  • CoreLocation: ask When-In-Use first, handle reduced accuracy, use CLLocationUpdate.liveUpdates() on iOS 17+; MapKit needs no API key and SwiftUI Map uses MapCameraPosition.
  • AVFoundation camera is manual session management; startRunning() off the main thread; PhotosPicker needs no permission and returns only selected items.
  • StoreKit 2: Product.products, purchase(), listen to Transaction.updates, verify, finish(), validate server-side; IAP is required for digital goods.
  • WidgetKit is timeline-based snapshots with App Group data sharing; Live Activities are server-pushed and have strict limits (verify).
  • Sign in with Apple is required with other social logins (4.8); name/email only the first time; revoke tokens on account deletion.
  • App Intents expose actions to Siri, Shortcuts and Spotlight; Apple Pay, HealthKit and Core ML each have their own capability and privacy rules.
